title: The 60-second node triage drill
goal: Learn the first commands you run on any slow node, and what each one rules out. You will create each bottleneck yourself, so you know what it looks like.

steps.text: Install the tools (already done in S2 - run again to be sure).
steps.code: sudo apt install -y sysstat stress-ng fio iperf3 ethtool

steps.text: Run the 'first minute' set on an idle system and save it as your baseline. Read each output: what is the column that matters?
steps.code:
uptime                 # load average vs CPU count (nproc)
sudo dmesg -T | tail -20   # kernel errors, OOM kills, NIC resets
vmstat 1 5             # r = run queue, si/so = swapping, wa = I/O wait
mpstat -P ALL 1 3      # per-CPU %usr %sys %iowait %idle
pidstat 1 3            # which process uses CPU
iostat -xz 1 3         # %util, r_await/w_await per disk
free -m                # look at 'available', not 'free'
sar -n DEV 1 3         # rxkB/s txkB/s per NIC
ethtool -S eth0 | grep -iE 'err|drop'   # NIC error counters (name may differ: ip -br link)

steps.text: Bottleneck 1 - CPU. In terminal 1 run the load, in terminal 2 watch.
steps.code:
stress-ng --cpu 0 --timeout 60s          # terminal 1
vmstat 1    # terminal 2: 'r' climbs above nproc, 'id' near 0
mpstat -P ALL 1

steps.text: Bottleneck 2 - Memory.
steps.code:
stress-ng --vm 2 --vm-bytes 85% --timeout 60s
vmstat 1    # watch free drop, si/so > 0 if swapping
free -m

steps.text: Bottleneck 3 - Disk.
steps.code:
fio --name=randw --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --size=1G --numjobs=4 --iodepth=32 \
    --ioengine=libaio --direct=1 --runtime=60 --time_based --filename=/tmp/fio.test
iostat -xz 1   # %util near 100, w_await grows
rm -f /tmp/fio.test

steps.text: Bottleneck 4 - Network (loopback in WSL; between the two VMs of S7 for a real NIC).
steps.code:
iperf3 -s &          # server
iperf3 -c 127.0.0.1 -t 30
sar -n DEV 1

steps.text: Write triage.sh - one command, one page, one verdict per resource. Start from this skeleton and improve it.
steps.code:
cat > ~/gpu-lab/linux/triage.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 60-second triage: prints a verdict per resource. Usage: ./triage.sh
set -u
N=$(nproc)
echo "== $(hostname)  $(date -Is)  cpus=$N"
LOAD=$(awk '{print $1}' /proc/loadavg)
RQ=$(vmstat 1 3 | tail -1 | awk '{print $1}')
IDLE=$(vmstat 1 3 | tail -1 | awk '{print $15}')
SWAP=$(vmstat 1 3 | tail -1 | awk '{print $7+$8}')
AVAIL=$(free -m | awk '/Mem:/ {printf "%d", $7/$2*100}')
echo "CPU   : load=$LOAD runq=$RQ idle=${IDLE}% -> $( [ "$RQ" -gt "$N" ] && echo SATURATED || echo ok)"
echo "MEM   : available=${AVAIL}% swap_io=$SWAP -> $( [ "$AVAIL" -lt 10 ] || [ "$SWAP" -gt 0 ] && echo PRESSURE || echo ok)"
DISK=$(iostat -dxz 1 2 | awk '/^[a-z]/ && $1!="Device" {u=$NF} END {print u+0}')
echo "DISK  : max_util=${DISK}% -> $( awk -v d=$DISK 'BEGIN{print (d>80)?"SATURATED":"ok"}')"
ERR=$(sudo dmesg -T 2>/dev/null | grep -ciE 'error|fail|oom|xid' || true)
echo "KERNEL: dmesg error-ish lines=$ERR -> $( [ "$ERR" -gt 0 ] && echo CHECK || echo ok)"
if command -v nvidia-smi >/dev/null; then
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,power.draw,clocks_event_reasons.active --format=csv,noheader \
   | sed 's/^/GPU   : /'
fi
EOF
chmod +x ~/gpu-lab/linux/triage.sh && ~/gpu-lab/linux/triage.sh

expect: Idle: all 'ok'. Under stress-ng --cpu: CPU SATURATED. Under --vm: MEM PRESSURE. Under fio: DISK SATURATED. Each tool exposes its bottleneck within a few seconds.
verify: You produced each of the 4 verdicts on purpose
You can say what vmstat r, si/so and iostat %util mean without notes

broke.fix: sudo apt install sysstat

broke.symptom: ethtool -S says 'no stats available' in WSL
broke.fix: Normal for the WSL virtual NIC - repeat on the VMs from S7
use sudo dmesg

commit: linux/triage.sh, notes/A1.md with a table: symptom | command | column to read | meaning
cleanup: Nothing running. Kill iperf3 server: pkill iperf3
interview: A node is slow. I run uptime, dmesg, vmstat, mpstat, pidstat, iostat, free, sar -n DEV in that order - USE method: utilization, saturation, errors per resource - and on a GPU box add nvidia-smi and clock-event reasons. Each one rules out a layer in seconds.

title: Build an XID decoder
goal: XID errors are how the NVIDIA driver reports GPU problems in the kernel log. You will build a tool that reads them and tells an operator what to do. No GPU needed.

steps.text: Open the NVIDIA XID catalog (link in Go deeper). Fill this starter table. Meanings below are the common ones - confirm each 'action' against the catalog before you trust it.
steps.code:
mkdir -p ~/gpu-lab/gpu-health && cd ~/gpu-lab/gpu-health
cat > xid_table.json <<'EOF'
{
 "13": {"name": "Graphics engine exception", "cat": "application", "sev": "low",  "action": "Usually app bug; check the job. Repeats on one GPU -> run DCGM diag"},
 "31": {"name": "GPU memory page fault",     "cat": "application", "sev": "low",  "action": "Illegal memory access by app; check app/driver"},
 "43": {"name": "GPU stopped processing",    "cat": "application", "sev": "low",  "action": "App-level; restart job"},
 "45": {"name": "Preemptive cleanup",        "cat": "application", "sev": "info", "action": "Follows a killed process; read the earlier XID"},
 "48": {"name": "Double-bit ECC error",      "cat": "memory",      "sev": "high", "action": "Uncorrectable; drain, reset GPU, check retired/remapped rows"},
 "62": {"name": "Internal micro-controller halt", "cat": "firmware", "sev": "high", "action": "Reset GPU; repeated -> RMA"},
 "63": {"name": "Row remapping event",       "cat": "memory",      "sev": "info", "action": "Recorded; reset GPU at next drain to apply"},
 "64": {"name": "Row remapping failure",     "cat": "memory",      "sev": "high", "action": "Drain, reset; persistent -> RMA"},
 "74": {"name": "NVLink error",              "cat": "interconnect","sev": "high", "action": "Check NVLink counters/fabric manager; reset; persistent -> hardware"},
 "79": {"name": "GPU has fallen off the bus","cat": "bus",         "sev": "critical", "action": "Drain node, reboot host, check PCIe/power; escalate to vendor"},
 "92": {"name": "High single-bit ECC rate",  "cat": "memory",      "sev": "medium","action": "Watch trend; schedule diag"},
 "94": {"name": "Contained ECC error",       "cat": "memory",      "sev": "medium","action": "App killed, GPU OK; reset at drain"},
 "95": {"name": "Uncontained ECC error",     "cat": "memory",      "sev": "high", "action": "Drain and reset GPU"},
 "119":{"name": "GSP RPC timeout",           "cat": "firmware",    "sev": "high", "action": "Reset GPU / reboot; check driver version"},
 "120":{"name": "GSP error",                 "cat": "firmware",    "sev": "high", "action": "Reset GPU / reboot; check driver version"}
}
EOF

steps.text: Write xidwatch.py. It reads kernel log lines from stdin (or a file), finds 'NVRM: Xid', and prints severity + action.
Make sample log lines in the same shape the driver writes and test.
steps.code:
cat > sample.log <<'EOF'
Oct 10 10:01:02 node7 kernel: NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:3b:00): 79, pid=0, GPU has fallen off the bus.
Oct 10 10:02:11 node7 kernel: NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:5e:00): 48, pid=1234, An uncorrectable double bit error
Oct 10 10:02:12 node7 kernel: NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:5e:00): 63, pid=1234, Row remapping event
Oct 10 10:03:00 node7 kernel: eth0: link up
EOF
./xidwatch.py < sample.log

steps.text: Add unit tests with pytest.
steps.code:
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate && pip install pytest
cat > test_xidwatch.py <<'EOF'
from xidwatch import decode
def test_79():
    d = decode("kernel: NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:3b:00): 79, pid=0, GPU has fallen off the bus.")
    assert d["xid"] == 79 and d["sev"] == "critical" and d["bdf"] == "0000:3b:00"
def test_non_xid():
    assert decode("eth0: link up") is None
def test_unknown():
    assert decode("NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:01:00): 999, x")["cat"] == "unknown"
EOF
pytest -q

steps.text: Later, on a GPU instance (S8), run it live.
steps.code: journalctl -k -f | ~/gpu-lab/gpu-health/xidwatch.py

expect: ./xidwatch.py < sample.log prints 3 lines: CRITICAL for 79, HIGH for 48, INFO for 63, and ignores the eth0 line. pytest: 3 passed.
verify: You can explain 79 vs 48 vs 63/64 from memory
Unknown XIDs do not crash the tool

broke.symptom: Regex finds nothing on real logs
broke.fix: Print the raw line; some drivers write 'NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:3b:00.0)' - the pattern already allows '.' but check spacing
Run pytest from the gpu-health folder

interview: XID 79 means the GPU dropped off PCIe - drain and reboot, check power/PCIe, escalate. 48 is an uncorrectable ECC error; 63 is a row-remap event that applies at next reset; 64 means the remap failed. I built a decoder that turns those log lines into actions.

title: Transformer and cluster arithmetic
goal: Infrastructure people must do the math customers ask about: does the model fit, how big is the KV cache, how many GPU-days. You'll build a notebook you can reuse in interviews.

steps.text: Create a notebook environment.
steps.code:
cd ~/gpu-lab/llm && python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate && pip install jupyterlab
jupyter lab --no-browser   # open the printed http://localhost:8888 URL in Windows browser

steps.text: Cell 1 - training memory (mixed precision + Adam). Rule of thumb: ~16 bytes per parameter (BF16 weights 2 + BF16 grads 2 + FP32 master 4 + Adam m 4 + v 4), activations extra.
steps.code:
P = 70e9
bytes_per_param = 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4
total_gb = P * bytes_per_param / 1e9
print(f'{total_gb:,.0f} GB total')                 # ~1,120 GB
for gpus in (8, 16, 32):
    print(gpus, 'GPUs fully sharded ->', round(total_gb/gpus), 'GB/GPU (80 GB cards)')

steps.text: Cell 2 - KV cache per token = 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes. Example Llama-3-8B-like: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, BF16.
steps.code:
layers, kv_heads, head_dim, b = 32, 8, 128, 2
per_token = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * b
print(per_token/1024, 'KiB per token')              # 128 KiB
ctx = 8192
print(per_token*ctx/2**30, 'GiB per 8k-token sequence') # 1 GiB
free_gb = 24 - 16   # e.g. A10G 24 GB minus ~16 GB weights
print('max concurrent 8k sequences ~', int(free_gb*2**30 // (per_token*ctx)))

steps.text: Cell 3 - training compute: FLOPs ~ 6 x params x tokens. Convert to GPU-days at a given MFU.
steps.code:
N, D = 8e9, 1e12
flops = 6 * N * D                  # 4.8e22
peak = 989e12                      # H100 dense BF16 FLOP/s (spec sheet)
mfu = 0.40
gpu_days = flops / (peak*mfu) / 86400
print(f'{gpu_days:,.0f} GPU-days -> {gpu_days/1024:.1f} days on 1,024 GPUs')

steps.text: Read the two books linked in Go deeper (JAX scaling book: roofline + transformer chapters; HF Ultra-Scale Playbook). Add one markdown cell per chapter: 3 bullets in your own words.
Optional: watch Karpathy's build-nanogpt walkthrough; run it later on a GPU instance so the words 'attention', 'layer', 'token' become concrete.
steps.code: git clone https://github.com/karpathy/build-nanogpt

expect: 70B needs ~1.1 TB for training state, so it does not fit on one 8x80 GB node without offload; KV cache for an 8B-class model is ~128 KiB/token; 8B x 1T tokens ~1,400 H100-days at 40% MFU.
verify: You can redo all three calculations on a whiteboard
You know where the 16 bytes/param comes from
You can explain why longer context reduces batch size

broke.fix: Use the full URL with token from the terminal; WSL forwards localhost automatically

interview: Can a 70B model train on one 8x80 GB node? Show the 16 bytes/param math: ~1.1 TB of state vs 640 GB HBM - not without offload or more nodes. For inference I size KV cache per token and back out max batch at a context length.

title: Draw the node from memory
goal: Know which GPU sits next to which CPU socket and NIC. Every performance discussion (NUMA, GPUDirect, NCCL) starts from this picture.
before: S8 with instance_type = g4dn.12xlarge (or any multi-GPU node)

steps.text: Bring up the node and log in.
steps.code:
cd ~/gpu-lab/infra/gpu1 && terraform apply -var instance_type=g4dn.12xlarge
aws ssm start-session --target $(terraform output -raw id)
sudo -iu ubuntu && sudo apt install -y hwloc numactl pciutils

steps.text: Collect the topology facts into one file.
steps.code:
mkdir -p ~/topo && cd ~/topo
{ nvidia-smi topo -m; echo; numactl -H; echo; lscpu; echo; lspci -tv; } > topo.txt 2>&1
for n in /sys/class/net/*/device/numa_node; do echo "$n $(cat $n)"; done >> topo.txt
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,pci.bus_id,name --format=csv >> topo.txt
lstopo-no-graphics --of txt > lstopo.txt
cat topo.txt

steps.text: Decode the nvidia-smi topo legend: X = self, PIX = same PCIe switch, PXB = multiple PCIe switches, PHB = same host bridge, NODE = same NUMA node across host bridges, SYS = crosses sockets (slowest), NV# = NVLink with # links. Write which GPU pairs are what.
Copy the files back to your laptop (SSM has no scp; simplest: print and paste, or push to an S3 bucket you own).
steps.code: aws s3 cp ~/topo s3://<your-lab-bucket>/topo/ --recursive   # needs s3 permission on the role; or just cat and copy

steps.text: Draw it (draw.io or Excalidraw): sockets, NUMA nodes, PCIe switches, GPUs, NICs. Write 3 rules, e.g. 'rank on GPU0 binds to NUMA 0 and NIC X'. Compare with the DGX/HGX H100 diagram from the SuperPOD docs (Go deeper) - learn that picture too.
Destroy.
steps.code:
exit; exit
terraform destroy -auto-approve

expect: On g4dn/g5 you'll see PHB/NODE/SYS between GPUs (no NV#) - that's the point: no NVLink, all GPU-GPU traffic over PCIe. Single-socket sizes show 1 NUMA node.
verify: You can draw an 8-GPU HGX node with 4 NVSwitches and 8 NICs from memory
You know what SYS means for performance

broke.fix: sudo apt install hwloc
Try another AZ: change subnet index in main.tf, or use on-demand for 1 hour

interview: On an HGX H100 node 8 GPUs connect through NVSwitch, each GPU pairs with a NIC under the same PCIe switch, split across two CPU sockets. GPUDirect RDMA traffic goes GPU->PCIe switch->NIC without touching CPU memory, so placement under the same switch matters.

title: DCGM diagnostics, levels 1 to 4
goal: DCGM is NVIDIA's data-center GPU manager. Its diag levels are how fleets prove a GPU is healthy. Learn what each level runs and how long it takes.

steps.text: Start a GPU instance (g4dn.xlarge is fine).
steps.code:
cd ~/gpu-lab/infra/gpu1 && terraform apply
aws ssm start-session --target $(terraform output -raw id)
sudo -iu ubuntu; nvidia-smi

steps.text: Check DCGM. The Deep Learning Base AMI already includes DCGM 4, so this usually just starts the service. If `dcgmi` is missing (plain Ubuntu), install the package that matches your driver's CUDA major version, as NVIDIA's DCGM guide does.
Run levels 1, 2, 3 and save JSON. Time each one.
steps.code:
mkdir -p ~/dcgm && cd ~/dcgm
for r in 1 2 3; do /usr/bin/time -f "r$r %e s" dcgmi diag -r $r -j > r$r.json; done
jq 'keys' r1.json      # look at the structure before parsing

steps.text: Read which plugins each level adds (the DCGM docs in Go deeper list them). Optional: r4 takes hours - skip on a T4 unless you want the experience.
Write a parser. The JSON layout differs between DCGM 3 and 4, so this walks the tree and prints any test name + result it finds - adjust once you've seen your file.
Also try health watches and live fields.
steps.code:
dcgmi health -s a          # enable all watches on group 0
dcgmi health -c
dcgmi dmon -e 150,155,203,204 -c 5   # temp, power, gpu util, mem copy util (field IDs)

steps.text: Copy results to your repo (print/paste or S3), destroy.
steps.code: terraform destroy -auto-approve

expect: discovery lists 1 GPU. r1 finishes in seconds, r2 in minutes, r3 tens of minutes on a T4. All tests Pass on a healthy GPU.
verify: Timing table r1/r2/r3 vs documented Hopper figures (Go deeper)
You can say what r3 adds over r2

broke.symptom: dcgmi: Unable to connect to host engine
broke.fix: sudo systemctl status nvidia-dcgm; start it; or run nv-hostengine manually
Some plugins need specific GPUs/NVLink - note it, that's a finding
The CUDA apt repo must be configured first (NVIDIA CUDA installation guide). On Maxwell/Pascal/Volta GPUs with driver 580 use the -cuda12 package

commit: gpu-health/dcgm_report.py, results/dcgm/<gpu>-r1..r3.json, notes/B2.md with timing table
interview: r1 is a seconds-long sanity check, r2 adds PCIe/NVLink and memory tests, r3 adds stress, power, bandwidth and NCCL plugins and takes ~30 min on 8 GPUs, r4 adds memtest/pulse for hours. I run r3 at acceptance and r1 at job start.

title: Redfish 101 on a mockup server
goal: Redfish is the REST API every modern server BMC exposes (power, temps, fans, logs, firmware). You'll learn it with no hardware using DMTF's mockup server.

steps.text: Run the mockup server. Easiest path is the published container (it ships a sample server); if the image name/tag changed, follow the repo README to run redfishMockupServer.py with -D <mockup dir> instead.
steps.code:
docker run -d --name rf -p 8000:8000 dmtf/redfish-mockup-server:latest
curl -s localhost:8000/redfish/v1 | jq .

steps.text: Walk the tree by hand. Follow every @odata.id link.
steps.code:
curl -s localhost:8000/redfish/v1/Systems | jq .
SYS=$(curl -s localhost:8000/redfish/v1/Systems | jq -r '.Members[0]."@odata.id"')
curl -s localhost:8000$SYS | jq '{PowerState, Status, ProcessorSummary, MemorySummary}'
curl -s localhost:8000/redfish/v1/Chassis | jq .
CH=$(curl -s localhost:8000/redfish/v1/Chassis | jq -r '.Members[0]."@odata.id"')
curl -s localhost:8000$CH/Thermal | jq '.Temperatures[] | {Name, ReadingCelsius}'
curl -s localhost:8000$CH/Power   | jq '.PowerSupplies[] | {Name, Status}'
curl -s localhost:8000/redfish/v1/Managers | jq .
curl -s localhost:8000$SYS/Bios | jq '.Attributes'    # if present in the mockup

steps.text: Write redfish_health.py.
Run DMTF's Service Validator against the mockup and read the report. Check its README/--help for the exact address flag of your version.
steps.code:
git clone https://github.com/DMTF/Redfish-Service-Validator && cd Redfish-Service-Validator
pip install -r requirements.txt
python3 RedfishServiceValidator.py --help | head -30
python3 RedfishServiceValidator.py --ip http://localhost:8000   # flag name per --help

steps.text: Read the IPMI vs Redfish comparison in the DMTF docs (Go deeper) and write 5 bullets.

expect: redfish_health.py prints the system with PowerState, temperatures with readings, fans and PSUs with Health OK. The validator writes an HTML report with pass/warn counts.
verify: You can name the 4 top-level collections (Systems, Chassis, Managers, UpdateService) and what lives where
Script handles a missing Thermal resource without crashing

broke.fix: Check the repo README for the current image name, or run the Python server from source with a mockup folder from DMTF's Redfish Mockups bundle (DSP2043)

broke.symptom: Newer schemas use ThermalSubsystem instead of Thermal
broke.fix: Add a fallback to /ThermalSubsystem/ThermalMetrics - good extension task

interview: IPMI is an old binary protocol with weak security and vendor quirks; Redfish is HTTPS + JSON with a schema, sessions and eventing, so hyperscalers automate fleets with it - inventory, power, thermal, logs and firmware updates from one API.

title: RDMA from zero on Soft-RoCE
goal: RDMA lets one machine write into another's memory without the remote CPU. It's what InfiniBand/RoCE/EFA give NCCL. Soft-RoCE emulates it in software on any NIC, so you learn the commands and concepts for free.

steps.text: Create the two VMs and open a session on each (two terminals).
steps.code:
cd ~/gpu-lab/infra/vms && terraform init && terraform apply
terraform output
aws ssm start-session --target <id-0>     # terminal A
aws ssm start-session --target <id-1>     # terminal B
sudo -iu ubuntu

steps.text: On BOTH VMs: install RDMA user space + the kernel module package that contains rdma_rxe.
steps.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y rdma-core ibverbs-utils perftest iperf3 linux-modules-extra-$(uname -r)
sudo modprobe rdma_rxe
ip -br link            # note the NIC name, e.g. ens5
sudo rdma link add rxe0 type rxe netdev ens5
rdma link
ibv_devices
ibv_devinfo -d rxe0    # state: PORT_ACTIVE

steps.text: Bandwidth test. A = server, B = client (use A's private IP from terraform output). If it can't connect, add -x 1 (RoCEv2 GID index) on both sides.
steps.code:
# A
ib_write_bw -d rxe0
# B
ib_write_bw -d rxe0 <A_private_ip>

steps.text: Latency test and size sweep.
steps.code:
# A
ib_send_lat -d rxe0
# B
ib_send_lat -d rxe0 <A_private_ip>
# sweep all message sizes
# A: ib_write_bw -d rxe0 -a     B: ib_write_bw -d rxe0 -a <A_private_ip>

steps.text: TCP baseline on the same pair.
steps.code:
# A
iperf3 -s
# B
iperf3 -c <A_private_ip> -t 20

steps.text: Write one page in your own words: queue pair (QP), memory region (MR), protection domain (PD), completion queue (CQ), and why RDMA saves CPU and copies.
Destroy.
steps.code: terraform destroy -auto-approve

expect: ibv_devinfo shows rxe0 PORT_ACTIVE. ib_write_bw prints a bandwidth table (Soft-RoCE is CPU-bound, so numbers can be lower than iperf3 - that is fine and worth explaining).
verify: You can say why real RoCE/IB numbers beat TCP while Soft-RoCE does not

broke.symptom: modprobe: FATAL: Module rdma_rxe not found
broke.fix: Install linux-modules-extra-$(uname -r); if your kernel flavor lacks it, use the generic kernel or a VirtualBox Ubuntu VM
Security group must allow all traffic between the VMs (S7 does); perftest uses TCP 18515 for setup and UDP 4791 for RoCEv2

broke.symptom: Failed to modify QP to RTR
broke.fix: Add -x 1 (GID index for RoCEv2) on both sides; check 'show_gids'

interview: RDMA moves data NIC-to-memory without the remote CPU or kernel copies, using queue pairs and registered memory regions. All-reduce sends huge buffers between GPUs every step, so the fabric must be RDMA (IB, RoCE or EFA) or the GPUs sit idle.

title: nccl-tests on one node and the busbw formula
goal: NCCL is the library that moves data between GPUs for training. nccl-tests measures it. Learn to run it, read algbw vs busbw, and plot results.

steps.text: Start a 4-GPU node.
steps.code:
cd ~/gpu-lab/infra/gpu1 && terraform apply -var instance_type=g4dn.12xlarge
aws ssm start-session --target $(terraform output -raw id); sudo -iu ubuntu; nvidia-smi -L

steps.text: Find NCCL and build nccl-tests.
steps.code:
find / -name 'libnccl.so*' 2>/dev/null | head     # note the folder, e.g. /usr/local/cuda/lib or /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests && cd nccl-tests
make -j CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda NCCL_HOME=/usr        # NCCL_HOME = parent of the lib folder you found
ls build/

steps.text: Run all-reduce across the 4 GPUs.
steps.code: ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 4G -f 2 -g 4 | tee ~/ar.txt

steps.text: Understand the columns: algbw = size / time. busbw = algbw x 2(n-1)/n for all-reduce (n = 4 -> x1.5). busbw is comparable to link bandwidth whatever n is. Check one row by hand.
Run the other collectives and compare algorithms.
steps.code:
./build/all_gather_perf -b 8 -e 4G -f 2 -g 4 | tee ~/ag.txt
./build/reduce_scatter_perf -b 8 -e 4G -f 2 -g 4 | tee ~/rs.txt
./build/alltoall_perf -b 8 -e 1G -f 2 -g 4 | tee ~/a2a.txt
NCCL_ALGO=Ring ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 1M -e 1G -f 4 -g 4
NCCL_ALGO=Tree ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 1M -e 1G -f 4 -g 4
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 1G -e 1G -g 4 2>&1 | grep -iE 'NCCL INFO (Channel|Ring|Tree|P2P|via)' | head

steps.text: Plot busbw vs size on your laptop (paste ar.txt into results/).
steps.code:
cat > ~/gpu-lab/nccl/plot_nccl.py <<'EOF'
import sys, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rows=[l.split() for l in open(sys.argv[1]) if l.strip() and l.strip()[0].isdigit()]
size=[int(r[0]) for r in rows]; busbw=[float(r[7]) for r in rows]   # out-of-place busbw column
plt.semilogx(size, busbw, marker='o'); plt.xlabel('bytes'); plt.ylabel('busbw GB/s'); plt.title(sys.argv[1]); plt.grid(True)

steps.text: A training loop with a deliberately slow dataloader.
steps.code:
cat > slow.py <<'EOF'
import time, torch, torchvision, torchvision.transforms as T, sys
W = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 0
ds = torchvision.datasets.FakeData(size=20000, image_size=(3,224,224), transform=T.Compose([T.RandomResizedCrop(224), T.ToTensor()]))
dl = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(ds, batch_size=64, num_workers=W, pin_memory=W>0, prefetch_factor=4 if W else None)
m = torchvision.models.resnet50().cuda(); opt = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), 0.1)
t = time.time()
for i, (x, y) in enumerate(dl):
    x, y = x.cuda(non_blocking=True), y.cuda(non_blocking=True)
    loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(m(x), y); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    if i % 20 == 0: print(i, f'{(time.time()-t)/20:.3f}s/step', flush=True); t = time.time()
    if i == 200: break
EOF
python3 slow.py 0 &          # num_workers=0
nvidia-smi dmon -s u -c 30   # watch 'sm' column dip

steps.code:

steps.code:
# skeleton
#!/bin/bash
rc=0
for d in $(lspci -D -d 10de: | awk '{print $1}'); do
  cap=$(sudo lspci -vv -s $d | grep -oP 'LnkCap:.*?Speed \K[^,]+, Width x\d+')

  echo "$d cap=[$cap] sta=[$sta]"
  [[ "$sta" == *"downgraded"* ]] && { echo "  DOWNTRAINED"; rc=1; }
done
exit $rc

title: Debug a hang and a straggler

steps.text: Straggler script.
steps.code:
cat > ar_loop.py <<'EOF'
import os, time, datetime, torch, torch.distributed as dist
dist.init_process_group('nccl', timeout=datetime.timedelta(seconds=60))
r = dist.get_rank(); torch.cuda.set_device(int(os.environ['LOCAL_RANK']))
x = torch.ones(64*1024*1024, device='cuda')
slow = int(os.environ.get('SLOW_RANK', -1))
for i in range(500):
    if r == slow: time.sleep(0.2)
    t = time.time(); dist.all_reduce(x); torch.cuda.synchronize()
    if r == 0 and i % 10 == 0: print(i, f'{(time.time()-t)*1000:.1f} ms', flush=True)
dist.destroy_process_group()
EOF
torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 ar_loop.py
SLOW_RANK=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 ar_loop.py     # every rank's step time jumps

steps.text: Hang: kill one rank mid-run and watch the others.
steps.code:
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO TORCH_NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1 torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 ar_loop.py &
sleep 20; pkill -9 -f 'ar_loop.py' -n    # kills newest rank
# observe: others block until the 60 s timeout, then error

steps.text: Read nvidia-resiliency-ext straggler detection and torchft docs (Go deeper); try their example if time allows.

expect: With SLOW_RANK all ranks slow down equally (collectives wait for the slowest). Killing a rank makes others hang until the NCCL/PG timeout.

broke.fix: Activate the venv; or python -m torch.distributed.run

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: time-slicing-config, namespace: gpu-operator }
data:

    flags: { migStrategy: none }
    sharing:

        resources:
        - name: nvidia.com/gpu
          replicas: 4
EOF

  -p '{"spec":{"devicePlugin":{"config":{"name":"time-slicing-config","default":"any"}}}}'

title: Find the bad node by bisection

steps.text: Simulation on your laptop: a fake 'run_allreduce(nodes)' returns low busbw if a planted bad node is in the group.
steps.code:
cat > ~/gpu-lab/nccl/bisect_nodes.py <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Group-testing bisection to find slow nodes. Replace run_allreduce() with a real Slurm/nccl-tests call."""
import random
NODES = [f"node{i:03d}" for i in range(200)]
BAD = set(random.sample(NODES, 1))
TESTS = 0
def run_allreduce(group):          # returns busbw GB/s
    global TESTS; TESTS += 1
    return 40.0 if BAD & set(group) else 90.0
def bisect(group, thresh=80, min_size=2):
    if run_allreduce(group) >= thresh: return []
    if len(group) <= min_size: return group
    mid = len(group)//2
    return bisect(group[:mid], thresh, min_size) + bisect(group[mid:], thresh, min_size)
suspects = bisect(NODES)
print('planted:', BAD, 'suspects:', suspects, 'tests run:', TESTS)
EOF
python3 ~/gpu-lab/nccl/bisect_nodes.py

steps.text: Note the subtlety: a group of 1 can't run all-reduce - pair a suspect with a known-good node to confirm. Extend the script to do that.

Real version: run_allreduce() submits `srun -N <len> --nodelist=<group> all_reduce_perf ...`, parses busbw, and also greps each node's dmesg for XIDs. Use the Slurm cluster from G3 or the 2-node pair.
Add a Slurm hook: flagged node -> scontrol update nodename=X state=drain reason='bisect-slow'.

expect: Finds the planted node in ~log2(200) x 2 tests (~15-20) instead of 200 pairs.
